scenarios.summary: Capture a changing list without losing spaces, empty entries or order.

solution:

teaching.prerequisite_note: Use quoted arguments, printf and for loops from earlier units. This lesson introduces Bash arrays; they are not portable sh syntax.

concepts.title: A variable can hold a list
concepts.text: An array stores separate values under one name. books=('Field guide' '' '*.txt') stores three values: a title, an empty value and literal text. These are elements, or entries in the list. The first entry has index 0, the second index 1.

concepts.title: Read one entry, count entries, or revisit all
concepts.text: ${books[0]} reads one entry. ${#books[@]} counts entries, including empty ones. Sole quoted "${books[@]}" gives each entry separately to a command or loop. The double quotes preserve spaces and protect wildcard text from filename matching.

concepts.title: Capture supplied values without inventing them
concepts.text: The practice example creates books itself; the lab does not supply it. The assignment supplies script arguments, not a variable named queue. Create your own queue with queue=("$@"). An empty list queue=() differs from queue=(''), which contains one empty value.

teaching.example:
books=('Field guide' '' '*.txt')
printf 'Books: %s\nFirst: <%s>\n' "${#books[@]}" "${books[0]}"
for book in "${books[@]}"; do printf 'Book: <%s>\n' "$book"; done
teaching.inputs: No arguments or supplied variables. The example creates books; a.txt exists only to show that quoted wildcard text stays literal.
teaching.try_change: Add a fourth title, then replace the list with books=() and rerun. Compare the count and the number of Book lines.

scenarios.title: Repair a queue that loses its tail
scenarios.summary: Change the next job while retaining the waiting jobs and an audit copy.
scenarios.objective: Repair the queue update. Script arguments are the original jobs; REPLACEMENT is a nonempty next-job label supplied by the lab. With no jobs print only Queue required plus a newline to standard error and return 2. Otherwise keep an independent original copy, replace only the first job with REPLACEMENT, and retain every later job unchanged. Print Original: COUNT, then Before: VALUE for each original job, followed by Revised: COUNT and After: VALUE for every revised job. All lines end with a newline. Preserve empty entries, spaces and literal wildcard text. Return 0 on success and change no files.

teaching.prerequisite_note: First complete Keep an exact dispatch queue. You will compare whole-list replacement with changing the first entry.

concepts.title: A copy stays available
concepts.text: original=("${stops[@]}") copies every current value, including empty entries. Later changes to stops leave original intact. Each entry is copied separately, so changing one list does not change the other.

concepts.title: One entry differs from the whole list
concepts.text: For an existing Bash indexed array, stops='Workshop' changes entry 0 and keeps later entries. stops=('Workshop') replaces the entire list with one entry. An ordinary $stops read also reads entry 0; it does not mean every entry.

concepts.title: Investigate the lost work
concepts.text: The example creates both lists itself. In the assignment only REPLACEMENT and the arguments are supplied. The starter already records an original copy; run it and find why jobs disappear. One empty job is still a job, so test the count rather than whether its first text is empty.

concepts.title: A printf format can repeat for several values
concepts.text: printf 'Original: <%s>\n' "${original[@]}" receives one separate value per array entry. printf repeats its format while values remain, so each entry gets its own labeled line. With no value arguments, printf still uses the format once with an empty %s; use a for loop when an empty array must print no rows. Both example arrays are nonempty.

teaching.example:
stops=('Depot' 'East gate' 'North gate')
original=("${stops[@]}")
stops='Workshop'
printf 'Original: <%s>\n' "${original[@]}"
printf 'Updated: <%s>\n' "${stops[@]}"
teaching.inputs: No supplied variables or arguments. The example creates a route list and a separate original copy.
teaching.try_change: Change stops='Workshop' to stops=('Workshop') and run. Explain why the two later stops disappear; then restore it.

solution:
configs=(*.cfg)
documents=(*.txt)
if [ -f "${configs[0]}" ]; then :; else
    printf 'Required configuration missing\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
if [ -f "${documents[0]}" ]; then :; else documents=(); fi
printf 'Configurations: %s\n' "${#configs[@]}"
for file in "${configs[@]}"; do printf 'Config: %s\n' "$file"; done
printf 'Documents: %s\n' "${#documents[@]}"
for file in "${documents[@]}"; do printf 'Doc: %s\n' "$file"; done

concepts.title: Keep groups separate
concepts.text: tables=(*.csv) selects matching virtual filenames and saves them as distinct entries in C-byte order. A filename containing spaces stays one entry. Use a second array for a different group rather than joining both lists into one string.

concepts.title: A missing match is not a file
concepts.text: With no matches, *.csv remains the literal text *.csv. It would misleadingly count as one entry. Test -f on the first saved name; when no file exists there, tables=() records an actually empty selection. Hidden files need an explicit leading dot and are excluded here.

concepts.title: Count saved entries, then inspect each

if [ -f "${tables[0]}" ]; then :; else tables=(); fi
printf 'Tables: %s\n' "${#tables[@]}"
for table in "${tables[@]}"; do printf 'Table: %s\n' "$table"; done

scenarios.title: Preview and publish a safe handover
scenarios.summary: Validate a whole batch before choosing console preview or saved output.
scenarios.objective:
Build a handover tool. Arguments are MODE, DESTINATION, then one or more source filenames in order. MODE must be preview or save; DESTINATION must be nonempty. Every source must be a nonempty existing filename, different from DESTINATION. On any invalid input print only Cannot publish handover plus a newline to standard error, return 2 and change no files. Validate the complete list before producing output.

The report is Handover, then Files: COUNT, each followed by a newline. For each source, append Source: NAME plus a newline and its exact file contents, retaining duplicates and empty source files. In preview mode print this report to standard output and leave all files unchanged. In save mode replace DESTINATION with the report and print only Saved: DESTINATION plus a newline. Return 0 with no success errors; preserve every other file. Supplied filenames are single filenames without folder parts or leading hyphens; nonempty source contents end with a newline.

Preview prints the report. Save uses > once and >> for later pieces. Function-call redirection remains unsupported: redirect the individual printing commands.

initial.source:
# Validate arguments and every source before any output or file change.
# Keep the saved source list available for preview or publication.

cases.name: Preview keeps old report
cases.stdout:
Handover
Files: 2
Source: west.cfg
ready
Source: east notes.txt
inspect

after./work/result.txt:
Handover
Files: 2
Source: a.cfg
a
Source: b.cfg
b

after./work/audit.txt:
Handover
Files: 3
Source: two words.cfg
100% *
Source: empty.cfg
Source: two words.cfg
100% *

solution:
if [ "$#" -lt 3 ]; then printf 'Cannot publish handover\n' >&2; exit 2; fi
mode=$1
destination=$2
shift 2
sources=("$@")
if [ "$mode" = preview ] || [ "$mode" = save ]; then :; else
    printf 'Cannot publish handover\n' >&2; exit 2
fi
if [ -z "$destination" ]; then printf 'Cannot publish handover\n' >&2; exit 2; fi
for file in "${sources[@]}"; do
    if [ -z "$file" ] || [ "$file" = "$destination" ]; then
        printf 'Cannot publish handover\n' >&2; exit 2
    fi
    if [ -f "$file" ]; then :; else printf 'Cannot publish handover\n' >&2; exit 2; fi
done
report() {
    printf 'Handover\nFiles: %s\n' "${#sources[@]}"
    for file in "${sources[@]}"; do
        printf 'Source: %s\n' "$file"
        cat "$file"
    done
}
if [ "$mode" = preview ]; then
    report
else
    printf 'Handover\nFiles: %s\n' "${#sources[@]}" > "$destination"
    for file in "${sources[@]}"; do
        printf 'Source: %s\n' "$file" >> "$destination"
        cat "$file" >> "$destination"
    done
    printf 'Saved: %s\n' "$destination"
fi

teaching.prerequisite_note: Combine argument validation, arrays, functions, status and safe redirection from earlier units. This is an independent practical capstone.

concepts.title: Separate a plan from its destination
concepts.text: A preview should show the proposed report without changing files. Validate the entire input list before either previewing or opening an output file; > replaces a file immediately, even if a later check fails.

concepts.title: Reuse an intact list
concepts.text: After saving mode and destination, shift removes those control arguments. Capture the remaining arguments as separate source entries. Reuse that list for validation, a correct count, and report generation. Duplicates still count as separate requested entries.

concepts.title: Choose where the same information goes
concepts.text: The example previews or saves a two-item checklist with different values from the assignment. Array variables and labels are created by the script. Only its mode argument is supplied. The simulator supports redirection on individual commands, not report > file on a function call; keep that limitation explicit.

teaching.example:
labels=('Cable check' 'Map update')
show() {
    printf 'Checklist: %s\n' "${#labels[@]}"
    for label in "${labels[@]}"; do printf 'Check: %s\n' "$label"; done
}
if [ "$1" = preview ]; then
    show
else
    printf 'Checklist: %s\n' "${#labels[@]}" > checklist.txt
    for label in "${labels[@]}"; do printf 'Check: %s\n' "$label" >> checklist.txt; done
    printf 'Checklist saved\n'
fi
teaching.inputs: One argument: preview. Virtual checklist.txt starts with an earlier note. The example creates labels itself.
teaching.try_change: Change the condition to compare $1 with save, then run with the supplied preview argument. Inspect checklist.txt and the console output; restore the original comparison afterward.
